vjimc-2011-cat1-01.title: Explicit polynomial, then a polynomial with infinitely many roots
vjimc-2011-cat1-01.body:
**(a) Yes.** $\frac{k+2}{k}=1+2\cdot\frac1k$, so $P(x)=1+2x$ works.

**(b) No.** Suppose such a $P$ exists. Writing $t=\frac1k$, the condition reads
$$P(t)=\frac{1}{2k+1}=\frac{t}{2+t}\qquad\text{for } t=1,\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\dots$$
Consider the polynomial
$$F(x)=(x+2)P(x)-x .$$
For every positive integer $k$, $F\!\left(\frac1k\right)=\left(\frac1k+2\right)\frac{1}{2k+1}-\frac1k=\frac{2k+1}{k}\cdot\frac1{2k+1}-\frac1k=0$.
So $F$ has infinitely many roots $1,\frac12,\frac13,\dots$, hence $F$ is the zero polynomial:
$$(x+2)P(x)=x\qquad\text{for all real }x .$$
Putting $x=-2$ gives $0=-2$, a contradiction. So no such polynomial exists.

**Answer: (a) yes, (b) no.** ∎

vjimc-2011-cat1-01.title: Power series and the identity theorem for (b)
vjimc-2011-cat1-01.body:
For (a), $P(x)=2x+1$ again.

For (b), on the disc $|t|<2$ the function $g(t)=\frac{t}{2+t}$ is given by the power series
$$g(t)=\frac t2\cdot\frac{1}{1+t/2}=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{(-1)^m}{2^{m+1}}\,t^{m+1},$$
which has infinitely many nonzero coefficients. If a polynomial $P$ satisfied $P(1/k)=\frac1{2k+1}=g(1/k)$ for all $k$, then the holomorphic function $P-g$ on $|t|<2$ would vanish on the set $\{1/k\}$, which accumulates at $0$. By the identity theorem $P=g$ on the disc, so the Taylor coefficients of $P$ at $0$ would be those of $g$ — infinitely many nonzero — impossible for a polynomial.

**Answer: (a) yes, (b) no.** ∎

vjimc-2011-cat1-02.title: The mean is always the second or third term
vjimc-2011-cat1-02.body:
**Answer: the limit always exists and equals $1+\sqrt2$.**

**Step 1: two possible relations.** Since $a_n<a_{n+1}<a_{n+2}<a_{n+3}$, the mean $m_n=\frac14(a_n+a_{n+1}+a_{n+2}+a_{n+3})$ satisfies $a_n<m_n<a_{n+3}$. It is a term of the strictly increasing sequence, so $m_n=a_{n+1}$ or $m_n=a_{n+2}$. Thus for each $n$ exactly one of
$$a_n+a_{n+1}+a_{n+2}+a_{n+3}=4a_{n+1}\tag{1}$$
$$a_n+a_{n+1}+a_{n+2}+a_{n+3}=4a_{n+2}\tag{2}$$
holds. Let $A$ ($B$) be the set of $n$ for which (1) (resp. (2)) holds; $A$ and $B$ partition $\mathbb N$.

**Step 2: eventually only one relation.** If $k\in B$ and $k+1\in A$, then
$$a_k+a_{k+1}+a_{k+2}+a_{k+3}=4a_{k+2}=a_{k+1}+a_{k+2}+a_{k+3}+a_{k+4},$$
so $a_k=a_{k+4}$, impossible. Hence after an element of $B$ all later indices are in $B$: either $B=\emptyset$ (so all $n$ are in $A$) or there is $n_0$ with $n\in B$ for all $n\ge n_0$. In any case, from some index on, the same relation holds for every $n$.

**Step 3: relation (1) for all large $n$ is impossible.** Then $a_{n+3}+a_{n+2}-3a_{n+1}+a_n=0$ for $n\ge n_0$, a linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial
$$\lambda^3+\lambda^2-3\lambda+1=(\lambda-1)(\lambda^2+2\lambda-1),$$
whose roots $1,\ -1-\sqrt2,\ -1+\sqrt2$ are distinct. So $a_n=C_1+C_2(-1-\sqrt2)^n+C_3(\sqrt2-1)^n$ for $n\ge n_0$. If $C_2=0$, $(a_n)$ is bounded — contradiction. If $C_2\ne0$, then since $|-1-\sqrt2|>1$ dominates, $a_n$ has the sign of $C_2(-1)^n$ for large $n$, so it changes sign — contradicting $a_n>0$.

**Step 4: relation (2) for all large $n$.** Then $a_{n+3}-3a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}+a_n=0$ with characteristic polynomial
$$\lambda^3-3\lambda^2+\lambda+1=(\lambda-1)(\lambda^2-2\lambda-1),$$
roots $1,\ 1-\sqrt2,\ 1+\sqrt2$. So $a_n=C_1+C_2(1-\sqrt2)^n+C_3(1+\sqrt2)^n$ for $n\ge n_0$, where $|1-\sqrt2|<1$. If $C_3\le0$ the sequence would be bounded above (the first two terms are bounded), contradicting unboundedness. Hence $C_3>0$ and
$$\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{C_1(1+\sqrt2)^{-n}+C_2\left(\frac{1-\sqrt2}{1+\sqrt2}\right)^{n}(1-\sqrt2)+C_3(1+\sqrt2)}{C_1(1+\sqrt2)^{-n}+C_2\left(\frac{1-\sqrt2}{1+\sqrt2}\right)^{n}+C_3}\longrightarrow 1+\sqrt2 .$$

**Step 5: the value occurs.** $a_n=(1+\sqrt2)^n$ is positive, strictly increasing and unbounded, and since $\lambda=1+\sqrt2$ satisfies $\lambda^3=3\lambda^2-\lambda-1$, we get $a_n+a_{n+1}+a_{n+3}=3a_{n+2}$, i.e. the mean of $a_n,\dots,a_{n+3}$ is $a_{n+2}$. So the hypotheses can be met, and the only possible limit is $1+\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $1+\sqrt2$.** ∎

vjimc-2011-cat1-03.title: Expand, swap sums, and use Euler's partition identity
vjimc-2011-cat1-03.body:
Fix $x\in(-1,1)$. All double series below converge absolutely (their terms are bounded in absolute value by $(j+1)|x|^{j+k}$), so the order of summation may be changed freely. We use
$$\frac1{(1-u)^2}=\sum_{j=0}^\infty(j+1)u^j\qquad(|u|<1).$$

**Left side.** With $u=x^{2k+2}$:
$$L=\sum_{k\ge0}x^k(1+x^{2k+2})\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)x^{j(2k+2)}=\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)x^{2j}\sum_{k\ge0}x^{k(2j+1)}\left(1+x^{2k+2}\right).$$
The inner sum is $\frac{1}{1-x^{2j+1}}+\frac{x^2}{1-x^{2j+3}}$. Hence
$$L=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(j+1)x^{2j}}{1-x^{2j+1}}+\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(j+1)x^{2j+2}}{1-x^{2j+3}}=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(j+1)x^{2j}}{1-x^{2j+1}}+\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{j\,x^{2j}}{1-x^{2j+1}}=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(2j+1)x^{2j}}{1-x^{2j+1}} .$$

**Right side.** With $u=x^{k+1}$:
$$R=\sum_{k\ge0}(-x)^k\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)x^{(k+1)j}=\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)x^j\sum_{k\ge0}\left(-x^{j+1}\right)^k=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(j+1)x^j}{1+x^{j+1}} .$$

**Euler's identity.** For $|x|<1$ all products below converge absolutely, and
$$\prod_{n\ge1}(1+x^n)=\prod_{n\ge1}\frac{1-x^{2n}}{1-x^n}=\frac{\prod_{n\ge1}(1-x^{2n})}{\prod_{n\ge1}(1-x^{2n})\prod_{n\ge1}(1-x^{2n-1})}=\prod_{n\ge1}\frac1{1-x^{2n-1}},$$
because the factors $1-x^n$ split into those with $n$ even and $n$ odd. Taking logarithms (all factors are positive),
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\ln(1+x^n)=-\sum_{n\ge1}\ln(1-x^{2n-1})\qquad(-1<x<1).$$

**Differentiate.** On every interval $[-r,r]$ with $r<1$, the termwise derivatives $\frac{nx^{n-1}}{1+x^n}$ and $\frac{(2n-1)x^{2n-2}}{1-x^{2n-1}}$ are bounded by $\frac{n r^{n-1}}{1-r}$, a summable bound; so both series may be differentiated term by term. This gives
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{nx^{n-1}}{1+x^n}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(2n-1)x^{2n-2}}{1-x^{2n-1}} .$$
With $n=j+1$ the left side is $R$ and the right side is $L$. Hence $L=R$ for all $x\in(-1,1)$. ∎

vjimc-2011-cat1-04.title: Smallest prime divisor of the orders
vjimc-2011-cat1-04.body:
Write $o(g)$ for the order of $g$. The three relations all have the form
$$g^{-1}xg=x^2\qquad\text{with }(x,g)\in\{(b,a),\ (c,b^2),\ (a,c^3)\}.$$

**Assume the claim fails.** Then $N=o(a)\,o(b)\,o(c)>1$; let $p$ be the smallest prime dividing $N$. Choose $x\in\{a,b,c\}$ with $p\mid o(x)$, and let $g$ be its partner from the list above. Note that $o(g)$ divides $o(a)$, $o(b)$ or $o(c)$, so every prime factor of $o(g)$ is $\ge p$. Since every prime factor of $p-1$ is $<p$, we get
$$\gcd\big(o(g),\,p-1\big)=1 .$$

**An element of order $p$.** Write $o(x)=pk$ and put $d=x^k$, so $o(d)=p$. Raising $g^{-1}xg=x^2$ to the $k$-th power gives $g^{-1}x^kg=x^{2k}$, i.e.
$$g^{-1}dg=d^2 .$$
By induction, $g^{-m}dg^m=d^{2^m}$ for all $m\ge0$: indeed $g^{-(m+1)}dg^{m+1}=g^{-1}d^{2^m}g=(g^{-1}dg)^{2^m}=d^{2^{m+1}}$.

**$g^{p-1}$ commutes with $d$.** By Fermat's little theorem $2^p\equiv2\pmod p$, and $d^p=e$, so
$$g^{-p}dg^{p}=d^{2^p}=d^2=g^{-1}dg .$$
Conjugating both sides by $g^{-1}$ (i.e. computing $g(\cdot)g^{-1}$) gives $g^{-(p-1)}dg^{p-1}=d$, so $g^{p-1}$ commutes with $d$. Of course $g^{o(g)}=e$ also commutes with $d$.

**Hence $g$ commutes with $d$.** Since $\gcd(o(g),p-1)=1$, there are integers $r,s$ with $r\,o(g)+s(p-1)=1$, so $g=(g^{o(g)})^r(g^{p-1})^s$ is a product of elements commuting with $d$. Therefore
$$d^2=g^{-1}dg=d,$$
so $d=e$, contradicting $o(d)=p$.

Thus $N=1$, i.e. $o(a)=o(b)=o(c)=1$, and $a=b=c=e$. ∎
